section.title: Feature-Level Specification
section.description:
- For every feature listed in Section 6.1, provide a detailed design using the same Fx ID and feature name. - Each subsection must match the feature ID, name, and priority defined in Section 6.1. - No additional features beyond those in Section 6.1 may be specified here. - Connect every Feature to the Section 3 end-to-end demo with one observable Demo checkpoint under Acceptance Criteria. - Write for a junior developer seeing the Feature for the first time. Use plain language, explain unfamiliar acronyms and domain or technical terms on first use, and make the actor, action, conceptual data, and user-visible result understandable without reading code. - When multiple participants or layers make a flow easier to understand visually, recommend a concise Mermaid diagram in 7.x.3. Prefer `sequenceDiagram` for request, data, and response flow across UI, API, data stores, and external systems. - Feature diagrams are optional. Their absence never blocks approval, saving, or completion. Keep them at product-requirement resolution and exclude modules, classes, functions, schemas, libraries, and algorithms.
- SCOPE — this section captures REPRODUCIBLE REQUIREMENTS, not implementation decisions: - WRITE here (the WHAT, reproducibly): what each user action must do, which layers it crosses (UI → API → data), what must be true for it to be correct (acceptance criteria, edge cases, error responses the user sees), and the VALUES AND RULES the result must honor — limits, quotas, retention periods, size caps, permission rules, allowed value sets and forbidden transitions, mandatory inputs, uniqueness, units — each with its number (where it has one) and basis (pricing policy, security rule, regulation). - DO NOT write here (the WHY/HOW — these belong to an ADR or to the code): why a particular library / algorithm / key design was chosen, alternatives considered, trade-offs, tuning constants, exact column lists, or framework-specific snippets. - Rule of thumb: if a sentence would still be true after the team swaps the database or the hashing library, it belongs here. If it justifies *that choice*, it belongs in an ADR. - The two lists split on one question: **would a developer picking a different value break the requirement?** "Max 20 turns per session" survives any rewrite, so it is a requirement and stays. "Connection pool of 10" does not, so it is a tuning constant and goes. The same question covers non-numeric requirements — allowed value sets and forbidden transitions, mandatory inputs, visibility rules, uniqueness, units: "a cancelled order can never move to shipping" stays, while the enum identifier holding that state goes (the set is the requirement, the name is the code's). Never soften a requirement into "reasonably limited", "an appropriate period", or "the status is managed" — this section is where it enters the pipeline, and blurring it here lets the implementation invent its own. - `/feature-to-adr` transfers every implementation-relevant Feature contract into one or several ADRs. After transfer, ADRs are the implementation authority and this PRD remains a legacy planning document. A later PRD edit affects implementation only when the user explicitly re-imports it and approves a semantic ADR contract change.

template.title: Feature Template
template.header: Feature ID: Fx | Priority: Must-Have / Should-Have / Nice-to-Have

subsection.title: User Story
subsection.description: - Describe the user scenario for implementing this feature. - Use this format: As a [persona], I want to [action], so that [benefit].
subsection.example: - As a new user, I want to sign up with my email, so that I can access the service.

subsection.title: User Flow
subsection.description: - Describe the user flow for this feature. - Keep the flow simple and concise. - Use terms a first-time junior developer can follow. Explain unfamiliar terms when they first appear instead of assuming product knowledge.
subsection.example: 1. Display a sign-up form with: - Email input field - Password input field - "Sign Up" button 2. When the user submits the form: - Validate input - Trigger an API call - Redirect to the main screen upon successful sign-up

subsection.title: Technical Description
subsection.description: - Describe the implementation as a vertical slice: trace each user action end-to-end from UI through API to data store, so this feature can be developed and tested independently. - For each key action in the user flow, describe WHAT happens at each layer it touches (UI / API / data) — at the level of behavior and responsibility, not implementation. - Make the explanation independently understandable to a junior developer seeing the Feature for the first time: identify the actor, action, conceptual data, and user-visible result, and explain unfamiliar acronyms or domain and technical terms on first use. - When multiple participants or layers make the flow easier to understand visually, recommend and normally include a concise Mermaid diagram. Prefer `sequenceDiagram` for request, data, and response flow across the user, UI, API, data store, and external systems. Use another Mermaid type only when state, branching, or conceptual relationships are clearer that way. - The diagram is optional and its absence never blocks approval, saving, or completion. It supplements rather than replaces the prose and must not repeat the entire flow. - Keep diagram participants and messages at product-requirement resolution. Do not include modules, classes, functions, fields, schemas, libraries, algorithms, or other implementation detail. - Stay reproducible, stay decision-free: - DO state: the action, the layers it crosses, the data it reads/writes (conceptually), what is returned to the user, any shared interface this feature relies on (e.g., "uses the shared auth session", "writes to the user record"), and any value or rule the result must honor (a limit, quota, retention period, size cap, permission rule, allowed value set, forbidden transition, mandatory input, uniqueness, or unit) with its number — where it has one — and basis. - DO NOT state: chosen libraries/algorithms (e.g., bcrypt, JWT), exact column lists, tuning constants (pool sizes, backoff delays, cache lifetimes), or why one approach was picked over another — those are architectural decisions (→ ADR) or implementation details (→ code), and pinning them here makes the PRD churn whenever the code does. - A requirement value is not a tuning constant: "a free-plan user may upload 5 files per month (pricing policy)" is a requirement and belongs here; "the upload retries 3 times" is a tuning constant and does not. - Requirements are not only numbers: allowed value sets and forbidden transitions, mandatory inputs, who may see what, uniqueness, and units are requirements too. "An order is one of paid / shipping / delivered / cancelled, and a cancelled order never moves to shipping" belongs here; the enum identifier that holds those states does not. - Keep API references at the endpoint level (method + path + purpose); leave request/response schemas to the code. - If this feature shares resources with other features (e.g., a common table or auth middleware), note the shared interface rather than redefining it.
subsection.example:
1. Submit Sign-up Form - UI (User Interface — the screen the user interacts with): the sign-up form sends the email and password to the sign-up endpoint (POST /api/auth/signup) - API (Application Programming Interface — the system boundary that processes the request): validates the input, rejects duplicate emails, and creates the user with the password stored in non-recoverable (hashed) form - Data store (where persistent account information is kept): a new user record is saved - Response: the user is authenticated and lands on the main screen 2. Validate Email (real-time) - UI: as the user leaves the email field, checks availability (GET /api/auth/check-email) - API: looks up whether the email is already taken - Response: an inline message tells the user if the email is available
Because account creation crosses several participants, this optional diagram makes the request, data, and response path easier to scan:
```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor User participant UI as Sign-up screen participant API as Sign-up API participant Data as User data store
User->>UI: Enter email and password UI->>API: Request account creation API->>Data: Check email and save new user Data-->>API: Account saved API-->>UI: Return authenticated session UI-->>User: Open the main screen ```
Values the result must honor:
- A password is at least 10 characters (security policy) - 5 consecutive failed sign-in attempts lock the account for 30 minutes (security policy) - An unverified account is deleted after 7 days (data-retention policy)
> (How the password is hashed, the auth token format, and the user table's columns are architectural/implementation choices — leave them to the ADR and the code, not this section. Retry counts and cache lifetimes are tuning constants and are likewise absent. But the three values above stay: a developer choosing different ones would break the product.)

subsection.title: Edge Cases
subsection.description: List potential edge cases and how they should be handled.
subsection.example: - User submits an already registered email → Show "Email already exists" error - User enters a password with less than 10 characters → Show validation error - Network timeout during API call → Show retry option

subsection.title: Error Handling
subsection.description: Define error scenarios and appropriate responses.
subsection.example: | Error Type | HTTP Code | User Message | |------------|-----------|--------------| | Validation failure | 400 | "Please check your input" | | Duplicate email | 409 | "Email already registered" | | Server error | 500 | "Something went wrong. Please try again." |

subsection.title: Acceptance Criteria
subsection.description: - Define the conditions that must be met for this feature to be considered complete. - Use clear, testable statements. - Restate every value from 7.x.3 ("Values the result must honor") as a checkable criterion, so the same number appears in both places and a reviewer can verify it. - End with one **Demo checkpoint** sentence that states this Feature's role in the Section 3 end-to-end demo and the observable completion result. - Do not repeat preconditions, user actions, or failure scenarios already recorded in User Flow, Edge Cases, and Error Handling.
subsection.example: - [ ] User can enter email and password in the sign-up form - [ ] Form validates email format before submission - [ ] Password must be at least 10 characters with one special character - [ ] A 6th consecutive failed sign-in locks the account for 30 minutes - [ ] An account still unverified after 7 days is deleted - [ ] Successful sign-up redirects user to main screen - [ ] Duplicate email shows appropriate error message - [ ] All error states display user-friendly messages - **Demo checkpoint:** This Feature completes the account-creation step in the Section 3 journey; completion is visible when the new user reaches the main screen as an authenticated user.
